title: The Trouble With Heat Pumps
summary: Sabine Hossenfelder argues that pro-heat-pump claims about old homes and owner satisfaction rest on selective UK samples, since most installs needed new radiators or other upgrades.

assertions.quote: They typically have half to a third of the energy needs of a typical fossil fuel heating.
an estimate from the USA says that they would go down by a similar factor
New heat emitters were needed with 93% of the heat pumps installed as the existing radiators would have been too small
heat pumps, at least so far, don't work well in old houses because they just don't get warm enough

verdicts.note: Envelope upgrades only slightly raise the share with positive NPV in cold climates and generally lower it in warmer ones; high-efficiency units avoid bill increases in 95% of homes without them.

RMI says electric space heating is less suitable in inefficient buildings, especially in cold climates, yet its leaky retrofit homes in mild Houston and Oakland still had lower heat pump energy costs.

LBNL: the cheapest high-savings approach paired heat pumps with only typical weatherization (attic, cavity fill, air sealing), while aggressive envelope upgrades cost double for modest marginal energy cost savings; basic weatherization helps, deep insulation was not needed.

Modeled savings depended mostly on house type and were largest in leaky/large homes (about $1,033/yr vs an 80% furnace in Duluth versus about $111 for a passive house); the table is garbled in extraction.

The UK study found no interaction between EPC rating and the heat pump's electricity increase, but because the grant required loft and cavity insulation, few homes in the sample were poorly insulated, so it cannot test the claim.

assertions.quote: They might reach just about 50 degrees Celsius or so while a typical gas or oil heating reaches 70 degrees or more.

verdicts.note: Standard air-to-water heat pumps run most efficiently at 35-55°C flow versus 60-80°C for typical boilers, though high-temperature models exist.

assertions.quote: Sweden, Norway and Finland lead the way in adoption with 40 percent of households using heat pumps already.

verdicts.note: Air-to-air heat pumps are the dominant heat pump type in Nordic and Baltic countries (Canada is not mentioned).
Edwards reports high heat pump penetration in Norway, Finland and Sweden; Canada is not covered and success is inferred from adoption.

Norway leads the world in heat pump penetration, with Finland and Sweden close behind and studies confirming real-world performance; elsewhere the report notes heat pumps heat 21 to 32% of homes in Canada's Maritime provinces.

assertions.quote: the heat pump owners we surveyed were demographically very different to the gas boiler owners

verdicts.note: The Nesta survey groups differed in property type and were self-selected, though monitored trials also report high satisfaction.
